topics.title: Prediction vs inference
topics.description: Prediction estimates an unseen outcome, while inference asks what relationships the data support; the goal determines the method and evaluation.

lessons.title: Two different questions
lessons.body: Prediction estimates an unknown outcome, such as next week's sales. Statistical inference uses sample data to learn about a broader population or a relationship, such as how sales differ between promoted and non-promoted weeks. The same data can be used for either task, but the questions are different.

lessons.title: Test a prediction
lessons.body: A sales forecast is useful when it predicts future sales accurately enough for a decision, such as ordering stock. Test it on data that was not used to fit or choose the model; for a forecast, keep the test period after the training period. Compare the errors with a simple baseline, such as last week's sales.

lessons.title: Estimate a relationship
lessons.body: An inference question might ask how average sales differ between weeks with and without a promotion. An estimated difference summarizes the observed relationship, while an interval can express uncertainty about the estimate under the method's assumptions. A narrow interval does not by itself prove a cause.

lessons.title: Watch for confounding
lessons.body: Promotions may occur more often during holidays, when demand would have been higher anyway. A sales difference between promoted and non-promoted weeks therefore does not automatically measure the effect of the promotion. A causal estimate needs a suitable study design and assumptions about other influences.

lessons.title: Match the method to the goal
lessons.body: A useful predictor can exploit an association even when that association is not causal. Conversely, explaining the effect of a promotion requires more than a model that forecasts sales accurately. Write down the decision, the target population, and whether the question is predictive, associational, or causal before choosing an evaluation.

topics.title: Features and targets
topics.description: Features are available inputs and the target is the outcome to predict; exclude information that would not exist at decision time.

lessons.title: Core idea and practice
lessons.body: A feature is an input used to make a prediction; the target is the outcome being predicted. In a demand forecast, past sales and calendar information might be features, while next week's sales are the target. An example in training pairs available feature values with an observed target.

lessons.title: Set the prediction time
lessons.body: Write down exactly when the prediction is made and what information is available then. For a loan decision made at application time, later repayment status is not a valid input. A field that was unavailable or updated later can leak information about the outcome.

lessons.title: Define the target
lessons.body: Specify the outcome and the time window precisely. 'Sales next week' needs a store, product scope, and consistent definition of a week. If different records use different windows or definitions, the model may learn an inconsistent task.

lessons.title: Check availability at serving
lessons.body: A field can exist in a historical dataset but be unavailable, delayed, or defined differently when predictions are served. Check its source, freshness, and meaning in both settings. Decide what the system should do when an expected feature is missing.

lessons.title: Evaluate without leakage
lessons.body: Build examples using only information available at each prediction time, then evaluate on held-out examples that reflect the intended use. An unusually accurate result may indicate that a feature contains information from after the outcome; inspect the data before assuming the model is excellent.

topics.title: Labeled examples
topics.description: A labeled example pairs input data with the outcome the learner should predict; label definitions must be consistent.

lessons.title: Core idea and practice
lessons.body: A labeled example pairs input values with the outcome a supervised model should learn to predict. For a delivery estimate, an example might contain shipment details available before dispatch and a label indicating whether the shipment arrived late.

lessons.title: Define the label
lessons.body: Write an explicit rule for assigning each label. For customer churn, 'cancelled during the next 30 days' is different from 'inactive for 30 days'. Record the observation window and how to handle customers whose outcomes are not yet known.

lessons.title: Gather and review labels
lessons.body: Labels can come from records, measurements, or human reviewers. Each source can contain mistakes: a cancellation record may be delayed, and reviewers may disagree on ambiguous cases. Use clear instructions and review a sample of labels against the source evidence.

lessons.title: Respect timing
lessons.body: The label is observed after the prediction point, but the input features must be available when the prediction is made. For example, a delivery's eventual arrival time can define lateness but cannot be an input to a forecast made before dispatch.

lessons.title: Check coverage
lessons.body: Inspect whether labels cover the populations and outcomes the system will encounter. A model trained only on labeled shipments from one region may not perform well elsewhere. Keep a representative held-out set and investigate missing or unreliable labels before trusting evaluation.

topics.title: Supervised learning
topics.description: Supervised methods learn a mapping from labeled examples to outputs, commonly for classification or regression.

lessons.title: Core idea and practice
lessons.body: Supervised learning uses examples with inputs and known target labels to fit a mapping from inputs to outputs. To predict delivery delay categories, each training example could contain shipment features and the observed delay category.

lessons.title: Choose the target
lessons.body: Classification predicts a category, such as on time or delayed. Regression predicts a number, such as minutes late. Define the target and its measurement window before selecting features or a metric.

lessons.title: Use available inputs
lessons.body: Select features that would be known at the time the prediction is made. For example, a planned route may be available before dispatch, while actual arrival time is not. Using a future value can leak the answer into training.

lessons.title: Fit and evaluate
lessons.body: Fit the model on training examples and evaluate it on separate examples that represent the intended use. Compare with a simple baseline, such as predicting the most common category. For time-dependent deliveries, a later test period may better reflect deployment.

lessons.title: Inspect mistakes
lessons.body: Review errors by route, time period, and other relevant groups when enough examples are available. An overall score can hide a recurring failure on a particular route. Investigate label quality and changes in delivery patterns before deciding how to improve the model.

topics.title: Unsupervised learning
topics.description: Unsupervised methods find structure without a supplied target and need human interpretation to establish usefulness.

lessons.title: Core idea and practice
lessons.body: Unsupervised learning looks for patterns in data without a supplied target label for each example. Common tasks include clustering similar examples and reducing the number of dimensions used to represent them.

lessons.title: Explore clusters
lessons.body: A clustering method groups examples according to a chosen representation and similarity measure. For support tickets, a group might contain related requests, but the algorithm does not automatically know the business meaning of the group.

lessons.title: Prepare the representation
lessons.body: The input features and their scale can strongly affect which examples appear similar. Choose features available for the intended use, handle missing values, and consider scaling where the method requires it. Different representations can produce different groups.

lessons.title: Interpret the result
lessons.body: Inspect representative examples from each cluster and look for mixed or misleading groups. Assign a descriptive label only after reviewing the data. A cluster ID is not a verified category or a prediction of a desired outcome.

lessons.title: Evaluate usefulness
lessons.body: Compare alternative settings and check whether the groups are stable enough and useful for the actual task. A mathematical clustering score alone cannot establish business usefulness. Watch for sensitive patterns and access restrictions when inspecting examples.

topics.title: Classification
topics.description: Classification predicts a discrete class; threshold choice and class-specific errors matter beyond accuracy.

lessons.title: Core idea and practice
lessons.body: Classification predicts a discrete category, such as whether a transaction should be reviewed. Some classifiers produce scores or probabilities that can be converted into decisions using a threshold.

lessons.title: Use a threshold
lessons.body: If a model assigns a positive-class score of 0.7 and the decision threshold is 0.6, the example is classified as positive. Changing the threshold can change which examples are flagged, even when the underlying scores stay the same.

lessons.title: Distinguish errors
lessons.body: A false positive flags a negative example; a false negative misses a positive example. In a screening workflow, both false alarms and missed positives have consequences. Assess them using representative labeled outcomes.

lessons.title: Look beyond accuracy
lessons.body: Accuracy counts all correct decisions, but can hide poor performance on a rare class. Precision describes the proportion of flagged examples that are truly positive; recall describes the proportion of positives that are flagged.

lessons.title: Choose for the task
lessons.body: Select a threshold using validation data and the costs of different errors. Evaluate the selected policy on separate held-out data, including important groups when feasible. Monitor outcomes after deployment because class prevalence and behavior can change.

topics.title: Regression
topics.description: Regression predicts a numeric quantity; error metrics should reflect the scale and cost of mistakes.

lessons.title: Core idea and practice
lessons.body: Regression predicts a numeric quantity, such as next week's units sold. The target, available inputs, and error metric should match the decision the prediction supports.

lessons.title: Define the target
lessons.body: Specify what is predicted, its units, and the time horizon. For a weekly sales forecast, use only features available before that week. Future information in training inputs can make evaluation misleading.

lessons.title: Measure error
lessons.body: Absolute error is the absolute difference between prediction and target. If a forecast is 12 units and the actual value is 9, the absolute error is 3 units. Mean absolute error averages these errors across examples.

lessons.title: Compare a baseline
lessons.body: A seasonal baseline might use sales from the same period in a previous cycle when that information is available. Compare the model and baseline on the same held-out periods, including operationally important errors.

lessons.title: Evaluate in context
lessons.body: Choose metrics that reflect the scale and cost of mistakes. Inspect errors across time and relevant groups, and check whether large errors have disproportionate impact. A low average error can hide poor performance in important cases.

topics.title: Train, validation, and test
topics.description: Training fits model parameters, validation supports choices, and a final test estimates performance after choices are fixed.

lessons.title: Give each split a role
lessons.body: The training set is used to fit model parameters. The validation set helps choose models, features, and settings, while a final test set estimates performance after those choices are fixed. Separating these roles makes it harder to mistake performance on familiar data for generalization. Each split should reflect the intended prediction task.

lessons.title: Avoid reusing the final test
lessons.body: Repeatedly checking a test score while changing a model effectively uses that test set for selection. The resulting score can become optimistic even though the model never directly trained on the test rows. Use validation data for iteration, then evaluate the fixed approach on the reserved test set. If a test set has guided repeated decisions, obtain a suitable new holdout when possible.

lessons.title: Split according to deployment
lessons.body: A random split is not always appropriate. For future forecasting, train on earlier periods and evaluate on later periods so the split matches the direction of time. If multiple rows belong to the same person or device, a group split may be needed to avoid placing closely related examples in both training and evaluation. Choose the split based on what will be new at deployment.

lessons.title: Fit preprocessing on training data
lessons.body: Preprocessing can leak information when it learns statistics from all rows before splitting. For example, a scaler should estimate its mean and standard deviation from training data, then apply those fitted values to validation and test data. During cross-validation, fit the preprocessing separately inside each training fold. Keep selection and preprocessing inside the evaluated pipeline.

lessons.title: Interpret the final estimate
lessons.body: A test score is an estimate based on a finite sample, not a guarantee of performance on every future group or period. Inspect class balance, important groups, and uncertainty when sample sizes permit. Data collected under a different process may not represent deployment, even if the split was technically separate. Document the evaluation population and its limitations.

topics.title: Generalization
topics.description: Generalization is performance on relevant unseen examples, not memorization of training records.

lessons.title: Core idea and practice
lessons.body: Generalization is performance on relevant unseen examples, not memorization of training records. Compare train and held-out scores using a representative split. This distinction should be checked against the data, users, and constraints of the actual task rather than treated as a guarantee.

lessons.title: Recognize memorization
lessons.body: A large gap between training and held-out performance can indicate that the model learned sample-specific detail. A small gap is not proof of good generalization if the held-out examples are unrepresentative.

lessons.title: Match the evaluation population
lessons.body: Define which future cases matter, then split data so that evaluation resembles those cases. For example, a model intended for new customers should be tested on customers not seen during training.

topics.title: Baseline models
topics.description: A simple baseline establishes a meaningful reference before adding model complexity.

lessons.title: Core idea and practice
lessons.body: A simple baseline establishes a meaningful reference before adding model complexity. Compare a demand model with last-week and seasonal-naive predictions. This distinction should be checked against the data, users, and constraints of the actual task rather than treated as a guarantee.

lessons.title: Choose a task-matched baseline
lessons.body: For numeric forecasts, predict a training-set mean or repeat the most recent seasonal value; for classification, predict the majority class. The baseline must use only information legitimately available at prediction time.

lessons.title: Use the baseline as a decision gate
lessons.body: Compare the candidate and baseline on the same held-out cases with a metric tied to the task. If the candidate does not improve meaningfully, investigate data quality or prefer the simpler baseline.

topics.title: Data leakage
topics.description: Leakage gives training or evaluation information that would not be available at prediction time, inflating results.

lessons.title: Core idea and practice
lessons.body: Leakage gives training or evaluation information that would not be available at prediction time, inflating results. Compute a time split before fitting imputers or selecting features. This distinction should be checked against the data, users, and constraints of the actual task rather than treated as a guarantee.

lessons.title: Find information from the future
lessons.body: A feature leaks when it records an outcome or event that occurs after the prediction decision. Check each feature against the exact time at which a real prediction would be made.

lessons.title: Keep evaluation data isolated
lessons.body: Fit data-dependent transformations using only training examples, then apply the learned transformation to validation or test data. Repeatedly choosing a model based on test results also leaks information from the test set into development.

topics.title: Class imbalance
topics.description: Rare classes can be hidden by high overall accuracy, so inspect per-class and prevalence-aware metrics.

lessons.title: Core idea and practice
lessons.body: Rare classes can be hidden by high overall accuracy, so inspect per-class and prevalence-aware metrics. A fraud detector that labels every transaction legitimate may still score highly. This distinction should be checked against the data, users, and constraints of the actual task rather than treated as a guarantee.

lessons.title: Read beyond accuracy
lessons.body: When positives are rare, a classifier can achieve high accuracy by predicting the majority class every time. Inspect the positive-class count and the errors the application cares about.

lessons.title: Choose a prevalence-aware check
lessons.body: Use precision, recall, or a precision–recall summary alongside a confusion matrix. Keep the evaluation prevalence representative because precision depends on how common the positive class is.

topics.title: Model assumptions
topics.description: Every model encodes assumptions about relationships, noise, and useful structure; check whether they fit the task.

lessons.title: Core idea and practice
lessons.body: Every model encodes assumptions about relationships, noise, and useful structure; check whether they fit the task. Inspect residual patterns before trusting a linear fit. This distinction should be checked against the data, users, and constraints of the actual task rather than treated as a guarantee.

lessons.title: Make assumptions explicit
lessons.body: A model's form constrains what relationships it can represent: a straight-line model cannot express an arbitrary curve without suitable features. Ask whether the chosen structure is plausible for the process being modeled.

lessons.title: Use diagnostics as evidence
lessons.body: Residual patterns, subgroup errors, and validation performance can expose a mismatch between assumptions and data. A diagnostic suggests what to investigate; it does not by itself prove a cause.

topics.title: Correlation is not causation
topics.description: Observed association alone does not establish that changing one variable causes an outcome.

lessons.title: Core idea and practice
lessons.body: Observed association alone does not establish that changing one variable causes an outcome. Do not infer that a discount caused higher sales from a simple correlation. This distinction should be checked against the data, users, and constraints of the actual task rather than treated as a guarantee.

lessons.title: Consider alternative explanations
lessons.body: A third factor can influence both a feature and an outcome, creating an association without a direct causal effect. Selection into the observed data can also distort an association.

lessons.title: Separate prediction from intervention
lessons.body: A feature can help forecast an outcome without showing what would happen if someone changed that feature. To estimate an intervention effect, define a causal question and justify a suitable study design.

topics.title: When not to use ML
topics.description: Rules, measurement, or process changes may be better when the task is stable, data is weak, or errors are costly.

lessons.title: Core idea and practice
lessons.body: Rules, measurement, or process changes may be better when the task is stable, data is weak, or errors are costly. Compare a deterministic eligibility rule with a learned model. This distinction should be checked against the data, users, and constraints of the actual task rather than treated as a guarantee.

lessons.title: Check whether learning is needed
lessons.body: A stable, explicit policy may be more accurate, transparent, and maintainable than a learned model. First determine whether the task has reliable measurements, enough representative examples, and a real need for adaptation.

lessons.title: Account for the cost of errors
lessons.body: When errors are severe or decisions must be explained, consider a human review, deterministic rule, or process improvement. Use ML only if it can be evaluated and monitored safely against those alternatives.

topics.title: Linear regression
topics.description: Linear regression estimates a numeric target as a weighted sum of inputs; residual patterns reveal where the model misses structure.

lessons.title: Core idea and practice
lessons.body: Linear regression predicts a numeric target using an intercept plus a weighted sum of features. A delivery model might estimate minutes from distance and load. Its coefficients are fitted from training data to minimize a chosen error objective.

lessons.title: Interpret a coefficient
lessons.body: If the distance coefficient is 2 minutes per kilometer, the prediction rises by 2 minutes for one additional kilometer while other included inputs are held fixed. This is a property of the fitted model, not proof that changing distance causes that exact change in delivery time.

lessons.title: Calculate a prediction
lessons.body: For a model predicting minutes as 10 + 2 * distance, a 7-kilometer route receives a prediction of 24 minutes. The intercept of 10 is the model's prediction when distance is zero; whether that is meaningful depends on the data and the task.

lessons.title: Inspect residuals
lessons.body: A residual is the observed target minus the prediction. If a delivery takes 30 minutes and the prediction is 24, its residual is 6 minutes. Examine residuals by route or distance: a systematic pattern can indicate missing structure, changing error variance, or data issues.

lessons.title: Evaluate on new data
lessons.body: Compare held-out predictions with observed delivery times using a suitable error measure and a simple baseline. Check errors across important routes and time periods, not only the overall average. Predictions far outside the training range can be unreliable.

topics.title: Logistic regression
topics.description: Logistic regression models class probabilities through a logistic link and supports threshold-based decisions.

lessons.title: Core idea and practice
lessons.body: Binary logistic regression combines input features into a score and applies the logistic function to produce a value between zero and one. That value is commonly interpreted as the model's estimated probability of the positive class, subject to evaluation and calibration.

lessons.title: From score to probability
lessons.body: The logistic function maps a score of zero to 0.5. Positive scores map above 0.5 and negative scores below it. A feature coefficient changes the score per unit of that feature, holding other inputs fixed; it does not add a fixed amount to the probability.

lessons.title: Choose a decision threshold
lessons.body: A threshold converts a model score into a class decision. Lowering the threshold generally identifies more positive cases but can also produce more false positives on a fixed set of examples. Choose it on validation data using the costs and constraints of the task.

lessons.title: Evaluate screening trade-offs
lessons.body: For a screening workflow, compare recall, precision, and the number of cases requiring follow-up across candidate thresholds. High recall can be useful when missed positives are costly, but follow-up capacity and false positives matter too.

lessons.title: Check probabilities and generalization
lessons.body: Assess performance on separate representative data and examine whether predicted probabilities are calibrated for the intended population. A value of 0.8 is not automatically a reliable 80% risk estimate. Data shifts and changes in class prevalence can affect performance.

topics.title: Decision trees
topics.description: A decision tree partitions feature space with sequential tests and can express nonlinear rules, but deep trees overfit.

lessons.title: Core idea and practice
lessons.body: A decision tree predicts by following a sequence of feature tests from a root to a leaf. The leaf supplies a prediction, such as a class or a numeric value. Different paths describe different regions of the feature space.

lessons.title: Follow a split
lessons.body: A delivery tree might first test whether distance is at most 5 km, then test traffic on one branch. Each decision routes an example to the next node. Features can be tested again deeper in the tree.

lessons.title: Learn from data
lessons.body: During training, a tree algorithm selects splits using a criterion such as impurity reduction for classification or reduced squared error for regression. The chosen rule depends on the training data and the algorithm; a split is not necessarily a causal relationship.

lessons.title: Control overfitting
lessons.body: A deep tree can fit rare patterns and noise in the training set. Limiting depth, requiring a minimum number of examples in a leaf, or pruning can reduce complexity. Select settings with validation data rather than assuming the deepest tree will generalize best.

lessons.title: Evaluate and interpret
lessons.body: Compare the tree with a simple baseline using a metric suited to the problem. Inspect held-out performance and important groups, and consider how missing values are handled by the chosen implementation. A readable path explains the model's rule, not why an outcome occurred.

topics.title: k-nearest neighbors
topics.description: k-NN predicts from nearby training examples, so scaling and the neighborhood size strongly affect results.

lessons.title: Core idea and practice
lessons.body: k-nearest neighbors predicts for a new example using nearby training examples under a chosen distance measure. For classification it may use a majority vote; for regression it may average neighbors' targets.

lessons.title: Find the neighbors
lessons.body: For a selected k, calculate distances from the new example to the stored training examples and select the k closest. The distance function and representation determine what nearby means. Ties require a defined handling rule.

lessons.title: Scale appropriately
lessons.body: When features use different units or ranges, one can dominate an unscaled distance. Fit any scaling transformation on the training data and apply the same transformation to validation and new examples to avoid leakage.

lessons.title: Choose k
lessons.body: A small k can be sensitive to noise, while a larger k can smooth local distinctions. Compare candidate values using validation data and a relevant metric. The best setting depends on the data, distance, and problem.

lessons.title: Consider prediction cost
lessons.body: A basic k-NN implementation stores training examples and searches them at prediction time. Consider memory, latency, and data access requirements as the dataset grows. Evaluate both predictive quality and practical constraints.

topics.title: Naive Bayes
topics.description: Naive Bayes combines class-conditional feature evidence under a conditional-independence assumption.

lessons.title: Core idea and practice
lessons.body: Naive Bayes is a family of classifiers that combines prior class probabilities with evidence from features. Its simplifying assumption is that features are conditionally independent given the class.

lessons.title: Represent a document
lessons.body: For a text classification baseline, represent each document using token counts or another appropriate feature representation. Learn the vocabulary and preprocessing from training data and apply the same transformation to new documents.

lessons.title: Combine evidence
lessons.body: The classifier estimates how likely the features are under each class and combines them with class priors. Smoothing can prevent an unseen token from giving a class a zero likelihood in common count-based variants.

lessons.title: Understand the assumption
lessons.body: Related words often appear together, so conditional independence is not always realistic. Naive Bayes can still be useful as a fast baseline, but correlated features can affect its probability estimates and decisions.

lessons.title: Evaluate the baseline
lessons.body: Compare predictions with labeled held-out examples using task-relevant metrics. Check class-specific errors and whether estimated probabilities are suitable for the decision. Avoid fitting the vocabulary or tuning settings on the final test set.

topics.title: Feature scaling
topics.description: Scaling aligns feature magnitudes for distance- and gradient-sensitive algorithms but is usually fitted only on training data.

lessons.title: Core idea and practice
lessons.body: Feature scaling transforms numeric inputs to make their ranges or units more comparable. It can matter for distance-based methods and gradient-based optimization, while its usefulness depends on the algorithm and features.

lessons.title: Standardize a feature
lessons.body: Standardization commonly subtracts the training mean and divides by the training standard deviation. For a training mean of 10 and standard deviation of 2, a value of 14 becomes 2. Handle constant features according to the chosen implementation.

lessons.title: Fit only on training data
lessons.body: Learn scaling parameters from the training split, then apply those same parameters to validation, test, and future inputs. Fitting on held-out data leaks information from evaluation into the training workflow.

lessons.title: Use a pipeline
lessons.body: Keep the fitted scaler with the model so training and serving use the same transformation. In cross-validation, fit a new scaler within each training fold. Record the transformation and its version with the model.

lessons.title: Check the effect
lessons.body: Compare held-out performance with a suitable baseline and inspect sensitivity to outliers or missing values. Scaling does not make all models accurate, and tree-based methods may not need it in the same way as distance-based methods.

topics.title: Missing-value handling
topics.description: Imputation estimates missing entries using training data and may need a missingness indicator when absence is informative.

lessons.title: Inspect missingness
lessons.body: A missing value may mean a measurement was unavailable, a question was skipped, or a field did not apply. Measure how often values are missing and check whether absence varies across groups or time periods. A blank is not automatically equivalent to zero. Understanding how missingness arises helps choose a suitable handling strategy.

lessons.title: Fit an imputer on training data
lessons.body: Imputation fills missing entries with a defined estimate, such as a training-set median for a numeric feature. Fit that estimate on training data only, then use the fitted value for validation, test, and serving inputs. For example, if the training median is 40, replace a missing validation value with 40, not the validation median. This keeps held-out information out of preprocessing.

lessons.title: Represent informative absence
lessons.body: Missingness itself may carry useful information. For example, an optional measurement may be absent more often for a particular workflow. A missingness indicator records whether the original value was missing, alongside any imputed value. Test whether this helps on appropriate held-out data; it can also reflect an unstable collection process.

lessons.title: Choose by feature and model
lessons.body: Mean, median, most-frequent-category, and model-supported missing-value handling have different assumptions and trade-offs. A median can be less affected by extreme numeric values than a mean, while an explicit unknown category may be suitable for some categorical inputs. Avoid assuming one method is best for every feature. Compare candidate approaches in a pipeline using validation data.

lessons.title: Monitor in production
lessons.body: A change in the missing-value rate can signal an upstream outage, a changed form, or a population shift. Track rates by important feature and, where appropriate, by group and source. Ensure serving uses the same fitted imputer and indicator rules as training. Investigate changes before assuming the model will behave as it did offline.

topics.title: Categorical encoding
topics.description: Encoding converts categories into model inputs while avoiding arbitrary numeric order for nominal categories.

lessons.title: Core idea and practice
lessons.body: Encoding converts categories into model inputs while avoiding arbitrary numeric order for nominal categories. Use one-hot encoding for colors rather than mapping them to 1, 2, 3. This distinction should be checked against the data, users, and constraints of the actual task rather than treated as a guarantee.

lessons.title: Distinguish category types
lessons.body: Nominal categories such as region have no natural numeric order, while an ordinal category such as low, medium, high does. Encoding should preserve the meaning of the category rather than introduce a false ordering.

lessons.title: Handle categories at prediction time
lessons.body: Fit category handling on training data and define what happens when a new category appears. One-hot encoding is useful for nominal inputs, but rare levels and high-cardinality fields need deliberate treatment.

topics.title: Train/test split strategy
topics.description: Random splitting suits independent examples; grouped or temporal splitting prevents related records crossing partitions.

lessons.title: Core idea and practice
lessons.body: Random splitting suits independent examples; grouped or temporal splitting prevents related records crossing partitions. Keep a patient's visits together when evaluating generalization to new patients. This distinction should be checked against the data, users, and constraints of the actual task rather than treated as a guarantee.

lessons.title: Identify dependent rows
lessons.body: Repeated visits from one patient or records from one device are not independent examples. If the goal is performance on unseen entities, keep every record from an entity in the same partition.

lessons.title: Respect the intended future
lessons.body: For future-facing predictions, train on earlier records and reserve a later period for testing. A random split can let future patterns inform training and give an unrealistic estimate.

topics.title: Confusion matrix
topics.description: A confusion matrix counts true and false positives and negatives, exposing error types hidden by accuracy.

lessons.title: Core idea and practice
lessons.body: A confusion matrix counts true and false positives and negatives, exposing error types hidden by accuracy. Inspect false negatives separately when missing a defect is expensive. This distinction should be checked against the data, users, and constraints of the actual task rather than treated as a guarantee.

lessons.title: Map decisions to counts
lessons.body: A true positive is a positive case correctly flagged, while a false positive is a negative case flagged incorrectly. False negatives are missed positives; true negatives are correctly rejected negatives.

lessons.title: Translate counts into consequences
lessons.body: Use the matrix to identify which errors dominate and who bears their cost. For a screening system, report the missed-case count as well as the number of cases sent for follow-up.

topics.title: Precision and recall
topics.description: Precision measures the fraction of predicted positives that are correct; recall measures the fraction of actual positives found.

lessons.title: Core idea and practice
lessons.body: Precision measures the fraction of predicted positives that are correct; recall measures the fraction of actual positives found. Prioritize recall for initial safety screening and review flagged cases. This distinction should be checked against the data, users, and constraints of the actual task rather than treated as a guarantee.

lessons.title: Read the denominators
lessons.body: Precision divides true positives by all predicted positives; recall divides true positives by all actual positives. A model can improve one while worsening the other as its decision threshold changes.

lessons.title: Tie the metric to the workflow
lessons.body: If every alert requires expensive review, higher precision may matter; if missing a serious case is unacceptable, recall may matter more. State the operational trade-off rather than treating one metric as universally best.

topics.title: F1 score
topics.description: F1 is the harmonic mean of precision and recall and is useful when both matter, but hides their individual values.

lessons.title: Core idea and practice
lessons.body: F1 is the harmonic mean of precision and recall and is useful when both matter, but hides their individual values. Report precision and recall alongside F1 for a spam filter. This distinction should be checked against the data, users, and constraints of the actual task rather than treated as a guarantee.

lessons.title: Understand the harmonic mean
lessons.body: F1 combines precision and recall and becomes small when either is small. It does not include true negatives, so it is not a complete summary of classification performance.

lessons.title: Report the components too
lessons.body: Two systems can have the same F1 but very different precision and recall. Show both component metrics and the confusion counts so that the operating behavior is visible.

topics.title: Cross-validation
topics.description: Cross-validation repeats fitting and evaluation across folds to reduce dependence on one split.

lessons.title: Core idea and practice
lessons.body: Cross-validation repeats fitting and evaluation across folds to reduce dependence on one split. Use stratified folds for a modest imbalanced classification dataset. This distinction should be checked against the data, users, and constraints of the actual task rather than treated as a guarantee.

lessons.title: Rotate the validation fold
lessons.body: In k-fold validation, each fold is held out once while the remaining folds train the model. Averaging the held-out scores gives a view less dependent on a single split.

lessons.title: Choose folds for the data structure
lessons.body: Stratify classification folds when preserving class proportions matters, and use grouped or time-ordered folds when examples are dependent. Cross-validation does not repair a biased or unrepresentative dataset.

topics.title: Regularization
topics.description: Regularization penalizes model complexity to reduce overfitting, trading fit against coefficient size.

lessons.title: Core idea and practice
lessons.body: Regularization penalizes model complexity to reduce overfitting, trading fit against coefficient size. Tune the penalty using validation folds, not the held-out test set. This distinction should be checked against the data, users, and constraints of the actual task rather than treated as a guarantee.

lessons.title: Penalize overly complex fits
lessons.body: A regularization penalty discourages large or numerous model coefficients, which can reduce sensitivity to training noise. Too much penalty can oversimplify the model and increase bias.

lessons.title: Tune without spending the test set
lessons.body: Choose the penalty using training-only validation or cross-validation, then evaluate the selected model once on an untouched test set. Repeated test-driven tuning makes the reported test score optimistic.

topics.title: Pipeline design
topics.description: A pipeline applies preprocessing and estimation together so each training fold learns transformations without leakage.

lessons.title: Core idea and practice
lessons.body: A pipeline applies preprocessing and estimation together so each training fold learns transformations without leakage. Put imputation, encoding, and the classifier inside one cross-validation pipeline. This distinction should be checked against the data, users, and constraints of the actual task rather than treated as a guarantee.

lessons.title: Bundle learned transformations
lessons.body: Imputation, scaling, and encoding can estimate values or categories from data. A pipeline ensures these steps are fitted on each training fold rather than on the full dataset before validation.

lessons.title: Preserve the inference sequence
lessons.body: Apply the same ordered transformations to new records that were used during training. Test the complete pipeline on realistic inputs, including missing values and categories not previously observed.

topics.title: Bias-variance trade-off
topics.description: High bias misses real structure while high variance follows sample noise; validation curves help locate a useful complexity range.

lessons.title: Core idea and practice
lessons.body: A high-bias model can miss important structure even when trained on representative data. A high-variance model can change substantially with the training sample and fit noise. For squared-error prediction under standard assumptions, expected error can be decomposed into bias squared, variance, and irreducible noise.

lessons.title: Compare model complexity
lessons.body: A shallow decision tree may underfit if it cannot capture important interactions; a very deep tree may fit quirks of the training sample. These are possibilities, not guarantees. Compare training and validation errors across tree depths rather than choosing a depth from the training score alone.

lessons.title: Use repeated validation
lessons.body: Evaluate candidate models across appropriate splits and inspect both the average and variation in validation error. For time-dependent data, preserve temporal order instead of randomly mixing future records into training. Use the same metric and splits when comparing candidates.

lessons.title: Choose a response
lessons.body: Underfitting may call for richer features or a less restrictive model; excessive sensitivity to the training sample may benefit from regularization, more representative data, or an ensemble. Diagnose first: data leakage, distribution shift, and label errors can produce misleading error patterns too.

lessons.title: Protect the final evaluation
lessons.body: Select complexity using training and validation data, then evaluate the chosen approach on a separate test set. Repeatedly choosing models based on the test score turns that set into another selection set. Report uncertainty and subgroup errors when the sample supports them.

topics.title: Ensemble learning
topics.description: Ensembles combine predictors to improve stability or reduce error; the benefit depends on member diversity and calibration.

lessons.title: Core idea and practice
lessons.body: An ensemble combines predictions from multiple models. Averaging numeric outputs or voting on classes can reduce sensitivity to individual models when their errors differ. Combining models does not guarantee an improvement.

lessons.title: Understand bagging
lessons.body: Bagging trains members on bootstrap samples drawn with replacement from the training set, then aggregates their predictions. High-variance learners such as deep decision trees can benefit because the average is often less sensitive to a particular sample.

lessons.title: Inspect diversity
lessons.body: If members make nearly identical mistakes, averaging provides limited benefit. Compare member errors as well as overall scores. Diversity is useful only when individual models also contain predictive signal; adding weak or unsuitable models can degrade an ensemble.

lessons.title: Combine predictions deliberately
lessons.body: For regression, an ensemble can average numeric predictions. For classification, it can vote on labels or average predicted probabilities; these are different aggregation rules and can yield different decisions. Evaluate probability calibration if the combined scores will be used as risk estimates.

lessons.title: Evaluate cost and quality
lessons.body: Compare the ensemble against a single-model baseline using the same representative validation protocol and metric. Include training and serving costs, memory, and latency. Use an untouched test set after selecting the approach.

topics.title: Random forests
topics.description: Random forests average decorrelated trees built from resampled data and feature subsets, often reducing variance.

lessons.title: Core idea and practice
lessons.body: A random forest combines predictions from multiple decision trees. The trees are trained with randomness in the examples and candidate features, which can make their errors less correlated than identical trees trained the same way.

lessons.title: Build diverse trees
lessons.body: A common implementation trains each tree on a bootstrap sample drawn with replacement from the training set. At each split, it considers a random subset of features. Exact sampling and splitting behavior depends on the implementation.

lessons.title: Combine predictions
lessons.body: For regression, a forest commonly averages tree predictions. For classification, implementations may aggregate class probabilities or votes. Combining varied trees often reduces variance compared with a single unstable tree, but it does not guarantee better performance.

lessons.title: Use out-of-bag evaluation carefully
lessons.body: A training example omitted from a tree's bootstrap sample can be evaluated by that tree. Aggregating predictions from trees for which the example was omitted gives an out-of-bag estimate when supported. Keep an appropriate independent evaluation set for final assessment.

lessons.title: Tune and assess cost
lessons.body: Compare held-out metrics with a baseline and tune settings such as tree depth, feature sampling, and tree count using validation data. More trees can increase memory and prediction cost. Check subgroup results and missing-value behavior where relevant.

topics.title: Gradient boosting
topics.description: Boosting adds learners sequentially to correct residual errors and can fit complex patterns, but requires careful regularization.

lessons.title: Core idea and practice
lessons.body: Gradient boosting builds an additive model in stages. Each new learner is fitted to improve the current model according to a loss function, often using shallow decision trees.

lessons.title: Improve sequentially
lessons.body: At each stage, the algorithm computes a direction related to the loss gradient and fits a new learner to it. For squared-error regression, this direction corresponds to residuals. Other losses have different gradients.

lessons.title: Control the update
lessons.body: The learning rate scales each learner's contribution, and the number and depth of trees affect model capacity. A smaller learning rate may require more stages. These settings interact and should be evaluated together.

lessons.title: Prevent overfitting
lessons.body: Complex trees or too many boosting stages can fit noise. Limit capacity and use validation-based early stopping where supported. Keep the final test set separate from tuning and early-stopping decisions.

lessons.title: Evaluate tradeoffs
lessons.body: Compare held-out metrics against a simple baseline and inspect relevant subgroups. Consider training and prediction cost, missing-value handling, and implementation details. Strong validation results do not prove a model will remain accurate after a distribution change.

topics.title: Hyperparameter search
topics.description: Search methods allocate evaluation effort across model settings; the final test set must not guide the search.

lessons.title: Core idea and practice
lessons.body: Hyperparameter search compares model settings such as tree depth or regularization strength. The search needs an evaluation procedure and a budget; the final test set should remain separate from tuning.

lessons.title: Choose a search strategy
lessons.body: Grid search tests specified combinations, while random search samples combinations from chosen distributions. Both depend on the search space and budget. A larger search is not automatically better if the evaluation data or metric is unsuitable.

lessons.title: Use validation properly
lessons.body: Fit preprocessing within each training fold and evaluate candidates on its validation fold. Select the setting using validation results. Repeatedly choosing based on the final test set leaks information into model selection.

lessons.title: Estimate a tuned workflow
lessons.body: Nested cross-validation uses an inner loop for tuning and an outer loop to evaluate the full selection procedure. Each outer test fold is kept out of its corresponding inner search. The resulting estimate can still have sampling uncertainty.

lessons.title: Record and assess
lessons.body: Record the search space, data splits, metric, random seeds, and selected settings. After choosing the workflow, evaluate the final fitted model on the reserved test set. Also consider training cost and stability across folds.

topics.title: Feature selection
topics.description: Feature selection can improve efficiency and interpretability, but selecting on all data leaks validation information.

lessons.title: Core idea and practice
lessons.body: Feature selection chooses a subset of inputs for a model. It can reduce computation or simplify interpretation, but removing a feature can also remove useful information.

lessons.title: Choose a selection method
lessons.body: Methods can rank features using training-data statistics, search subsets, or use selection built into a model. Each method has assumptions and cost. A selected feature is not automatically causal or useful in every deployment.

lessons.title: Avoid leakage
lessons.body: Fit the selector using only each cross-validation training fold, then apply it to the corresponding validation fold. Selecting features once using all available examples lets validation information influence the selected subset.

lessons.title: Assess stability
lessons.body: Compare selected features and validation scores across folds or resamples. Highly correlated features may be interchangeable, so a selected subset can vary even when predictive performance is similar.

lessons.title: Evaluate the workflow
lessons.body: Compare the complete selection-and-model pipeline with a suitable baseline on held-out data. Record selected features and transformation versions for serving. Check cost, missing-feature behavior, and relevant subgroup results.

topics.title: Probability calibration
topics.description: Calibration aligns predicted probabilities with empirical frequencies and is distinct from ranking quality.

lessons.title: Interpret calibration
lessons.body: A probabilistic classifier is calibrated when predicted probabilities agree with observed frequencies in the relevant population. Among many cases assigned about 0.7, roughly 70% should be positive if the model is calibrated at that level. This is a population statement, not a guarantee for an individual case. Calibration can differ between groups or change over time.

lessons.title: Separate ranking and calibration
lessons.body: A model may rank positive cases above negative cases well while giving probabilities that are systematically too high or too low. Ranking metrics such as ROC AUC and probability calibration answer different questions. A score transformation can preserve ranking while changing probability values. Evaluate both when decisions depend on risk estimates as well as ordering.

lessons.title: Inspect reliability
lessons.body: A reliability diagram groups predictions into probability ranges and compares average prediction with observed positive frequency in each group. Small groups have noisy frequency estimates, and the choice of bins affects the picture. Use a held-out evaluation set and consider uncertainty rather than treating every visible difference as a real change. Examine important populations where sufficient data is available.

lessons.title: Fit a calibration method
lessons.body: Methods such as sigmoid scaling and isotonic regression can map model scores to adjusted probabilities. Fit the calibrator using data separate from the data used to fit the underlying model, or use a properly designed cross-validation procedure. Select the method on validation evidence, then reserve a separate test for final evaluation. Small calibration sets can make flexible methods unstable.

lessons.title: Monitor after deployment
lessons.body: Evaluate calibration and proper scoring rules on held-out outcomes, and monitor again once production labels arrive. Brier score and log loss reflect probability quality but are not pure measures of calibration alone. Population shift, label delay, and selection effects can change the observed relationship between predictions and outcomes. Compare the intended deployment population and document uncertainty.

topics.title: ROC and precision-recall curves
topics.description: ROC summarizes ranking over thresholds; precision-recall plots are often more revealing when positives are rare.

lessons.title: Core idea and practice
lessons.body: ROC summarizes ranking over thresholds; precision-recall plots are often more revealing when positives are rare. Compare average precision at the operational class prevalence. This distinction should be checked against the data, users, and constraints of the actual task rather than treated as a guarantee.

lessons.title: Interpret the axes and prevalence
lessons.body: ROC plots true-positive rate against false-positive rate across thresholds, while a precision–recall curve tracks positive predictive value and recall. The latter makes the precision cost of rare positives especially visible.

lessons.title: Compare models at the right operating point
lessons.body: A curve summarizes threshold choices but does not choose an operational threshold for you. Compare performance at the expected prevalence and at the review capacity or error cost that the application can support.

topics.title: Threshold selection
topics.description: A classifier threshold maps scores to actions and should reflect error costs and capacity constraints.

lessons.title: Core idea and practice
lessons.body: A classifier threshold maps scores to actions and should reflect error costs and capacity constraints. Choose a threshold using validation costs, then freeze it before testing. This distinction should be checked against the data, users, and constraints of the actual task rather than treated as a guarantee.

lessons.title: Separate scores from decisions
lessons.body: A classifier score ranks or estimates risk; a threshold turns that score into an action. Changing the threshold can alter precision and recall without changing the model's ranking.

lessons.title: Select using development data
lessons.body: Estimate the cost or capacity trade-off on validation data, document the chosen threshold, and freeze it before final testing. Revisit the threshold if prevalence, costs, or available review capacity changes.

topics.title: Uncertainty and intervals
topics.description: Prediction intervals express outcome uncertainty under assumptions and can widen under sparse data or distribution shift.

lessons.title: Core idea and practice
lessons.body: Prediction intervals express outcome uncertainty under assumptions and can widen under sparse data or distribution shift. Communicate a range for demand forecasts instead of only a point estimate. This distinction should be checked against the data, users, and constraints of the actual task rather than treated as a guarantee.

lessons.title: Distinguish interval meanings
lessons.body: A confidence interval for a mean and a prediction interval for a future individual describe different uncertainty. Prediction intervals generally include both uncertainty in the estimated relationship and individual outcome variation.

lessons.title: Check coverage in relevant slices
lessons.body: Measure how often held-out outcomes fall inside intervals, including across important subgroups or time periods. A nominal coverage target is not a guarantee under distribution shift or a misspecified model.

topics.title: Unsupervised clustering validation
topics.description: Cluster scores summarize geometric structure but do not prove that groups are useful or stable.

lessons.title: Core idea and practice
lessons.body: Cluster scores summarize geometric structure but do not prove that groups are useful or stable. Review cluster examples and downstream utility in addition to silhouette score. This distinction should be checked against the data, users, and constraints of the actual task rather than treated as a guarantee.

lessons.title: Test stability and geometry
lessons.body: A cluster score such as silhouette summarizes geometric separation under a chosen distance, not whether the groups are real or useful. Check whether assignments persist across reasonable resamples and preprocessing choices.

lessons.title: Validate downstream meaning
lessons.body: Inspect representative members and ask whether the groups support a legitimate decision or useful description. If a cluster is unstable or not actionable, a higher geometric score alone is not a reason to deploy it.

topics.title: Principal component analysis
topics.description: PCA creates orthogonal directions of maximal variance after scaling, but high variance is not necessarily predictive signal.

lessons.title: Core idea and practice
lessons.body: PCA creates orthogonal directions of maximal variance after scaling, but high variance is not necessarily predictive signal. Fit PCA inside the training pipeline and examine explained variance. This distinction should be checked against the data, users, and constraints of the actual task rather than treated as a guarantee.

lessons.title: Understand variance directions
lessons.body: PCA forms orthogonal linear combinations ordered by the variance they explain. A direction with large feature variance is not necessarily important for predicting a target or preserving a rare but meaningful signal.

lessons.title: Fit PCA without leakage
lessons.body: Scale and fit PCA within the training pipeline, then apply the learned projection to held-out examples. Examine explained variance and downstream validation performance before choosing the number of components.

topics.title: Imbalanced learning
topics.description: Resampling, class weights, and thresholding address imbalance differently and must be applied without contaminating validation.

lessons.title: Core idea and practice
lessons.body: Resampling, class weights, and thresholding address imbalance differently and must be applied without contaminating validation. Resample only within training folds and report minority-class recall. This distinction should be checked against the data, users, and constraints of the actual task rather than treated as a guarantee.

lessons.title: Separate imbalance interventions
lessons.body: Class weighting changes the training loss, resampling changes the training examples, and threshold selection changes the final action rule. They address different parts of the problem and can be evaluated separately.

lessons.title: Keep the holdout natural
lessons.body: Resample or augment only within training folds; do not rebalance the validation or test set when estimating performance at real-world prevalence. Report precision and recall at that prevalence.

topics.title: Fairness evaluation
topics.description: Group metrics can reveal disparities but depend on target quality, group definitions, and the harms under review.

lessons.title: Core idea and practice
lessons.body: Group metrics can reveal disparities but depend on target quality, group definitions, and the harms under review. Compare false-negative rates across relevant populations and investigate causes. This distinction should be checked against the data, users, and constraints of the actual task rather than treated as a guarantee.

lessons.title: Choose a harm-relevant measure
lessons.body: Compare outcome quality and error rates across groups relevant to the decision, such as false-negative rates when missed cases are harmful. The correct groups and measures depend on the context and affected people.

lessons.title: Investigate before interpreting
lessons.body: A disparity can reflect measurement quality, sampling, label definitions, or the decision process. Validate labels and subgroup sample sizes, then investigate mechanisms instead of treating a metric gap as a complete explanation.

topics.title: Error analysis
topics.description: Segmented error review turns aggregate scores into actionable hypotheses about model failures.

lessons.title: Core idea and practice
lessons.body: Segmented error review turns aggregate scores into actionable hypotheses about model failures. Review false positives by source system before changing features. This distinction should be checked against the data, users, and constraints of the actual task rather than treated as a guarantee.

lessons.title: Turn errors into hypotheses
lessons.body: Review false positives and false negatives in meaningful slices such as source, time, or input quality. Look for recurring failure modes rather than changing the model in response to a single anecdote.

lessons.title: Verify the proposed fix
lessons.body: Form a specific hypothesis, make a controlled change, and compare it on the same validation design. Keep the final test set untouched while investigating and record any new trade-offs.

topics.title: Causal inference vs prediction
topics.description: Causal estimates require identification assumptions and design, not just predictive accuracy or feature importance.

lessons.title: Core idea and practice
lessons.body: Prediction asks what outcome is likely given observed features. Causal inference asks how an outcome would change under different interventions. A model can predict well using a proxy without estimating the effect of changing that proxy.

lessons.title: Define the estimand
lessons.body: Specify the population, intervention, comparison, outcome, and time horizon. For example, estimate the average effect of offering a training program versus not offering it on employment after six months. This differs from predicting employment among people who chose to enroll.

lessons.title: Account for confounding
lessons.body: Participants who enroll voluntarily may differ in motivation or prior experience, which can affect both enrollment and outcomes. Comparing their average outcomes with nonparticipants therefore need not isolate the program's effect. A causal diagram can help state which variables are assumed to influence treatment and outcome.

lessons.title: Select an identification design
lessons.body: Random assignment can support a causal comparison when implemented and analyzed appropriately. In observational data, methods such as adjustment or a defensible quasi-experiment rely on explicit assumptions, such as adequate overlap and no unmeasured confounding for a given adjustment strategy. Check the assumptions and their limitations.

lessons.title: Report uncertainty and limits
lessons.body: State the estimated effect, uncertainty interval, population, design, and plausible threats to identification. Sensitivity analyses can show how conclusions depend on assumptions but cannot verify an unobserved confounder is absent. Good predictive accuracy alone does not establish a causal effect.

topics.title: Distribution shift
topics.description: Covariate, label, and concept shift describe different changes and call for different diagnostics and responses.

lessons.title: Core idea and practice
lessons.body: Distribution shift occurs when the data encountered after training differs from the data used to develop the model. Changes can affect inputs, outcomes, or the relationship between them; the right response depends on what changed and how the model is used.

lessons.title: Identify covariate shift
lessons.body: Covariate shift refers to a change in the input distribution P(X) while the conditional relationship P(Y|X) remains unchanged under the formal assumption. For example, delivery routes may become longer. Input drift alone does not establish whether model performance has changed.

lessons.title: Identify label shift
lessons.body: Label shift refers to a change in the outcome distribution P(Y) while P(X|Y) remains unchanged under the label-shift assumption. A changing positive-class rate can affect precision even if some other metrics stay stable. These assumptions should be examined, not inferred from a single alert.

lessons.title: Investigate concept shift
lessons.body: Concept shift changes the relationship P(Y|X). For example, a route with the same observed features may have a different delay probability after a policy change. Detecting the impact typically requires outcomes or other evidence, which may arrive later than input data.

lessons.title: Respond with evidence
lessons.body: Track data quality and input distributions, then evaluate performance when representative labels arrive. Investigate measurement changes and subgroup effects before choosing a response such as recalibration, retraining, or rollback. Retraining on new data is not automatically safe or effective.

topics.title: Conformal prediction
topics.description: Conformal methods can provide finite-sample marginal coverage under exchangeability, but coverage can fail under shift.

lessons.title: Core idea and practice
lessons.body: Conformal prediction uses calibration data to construct prediction sets or intervals. Under exchangeability and the method's conditions, it can provide a finite-sample marginal coverage guarantee for a new example.

lessons.title: Calibrate uncertainty
lessons.body: In split conformal regression, fit a model on training data and compute nonconformity scores, such as absolute residuals, on separate calibration examples. Choose the appropriate finite-sample quantile for the target miscoverage rate, then use it to form intervals.

lessons.title: Interpret coverage
lessons.body: A 90% marginal coverage target concerns coverage across future examples under the stated assumptions; it does not mean every subgroup or every individual receives 90% conditional coverage. Interval width and usefulness matter alongside overall coverage.

lessons.title: Evaluate on held-out data
lessons.body: Use data separate from model fitting and calibration to estimate empirical coverage and interval width. Examine relevant groups and uncertainty in the estimate. A small evaluation sample can make observed coverage noisy.

lessons.title: Watch for distribution shift
lessons.body: The guarantee relies on assumptions such as exchangeability between calibration and future examples. Changes in inputs, outcomes, or collection can break those assumptions. Monitor delayed outcomes and coverage, investigate changes, and recalibrate or redesign when appropriate.

topics.title: Survival analysis
topics.description: Survival models account for event timing and right-censoring rather than treating unobserved events as negatives.

lessons.title: Core idea and practice
lessons.body: Survival analysis models time until a defined event, such as equipment failure. It can use information from units whose event has not been observed by the end of follow-up.

lessons.title: Understand right-censoring
lessons.body: If a machine remains operational when observation ends, its failure time is unknown but exceeds its observed follow-up time. This is right-censoring; it is not evidence that the machine will never fail.

lessons.title: Define time and event
lessons.body: Specify the start of observation, event definition, time units, and censoring rule before fitting a model. For example, record operating days until failure or study end. Changes in entry or observation practices can affect interpretation.

lessons.title: Interpret survival probability
lessons.body: A survival curve describes the probability that the event time exceeds a given time under the model or estimator. It concerns a population or specified covariates, not certainty about one machine. Confidence and assumptions should be considered.

lessons.title: Evaluate with censoring in mind
lessons.body: Use an appropriate held-out evaluation and metrics that account for censoring. Consider whether censoring is informative and whether follow-up differs across groups. A model can be misleading if the data collection process violates its assumptions.

topics.title: Count models
topics.description: Poisson and negative-binomial models represent counts with different dispersion assumptions.

lessons.title: Core idea and practice
lessons.body: Count models predict nonnegative event counts, such as incidents in a time interval. Poisson and negative-binomial models use different assumptions about how counts vary.

lessons.title: Consider exposure
lessons.body: Counts collected over different observation durations or population sizes are not directly comparable without accounting for exposure. A count regression may include the logarithm of exposure as an offset when its assumptions are appropriate.

lessons.title: Understand Poisson variation
lessons.body: A Poisson distribution has equal mean and variance for a given parameter. In regression, assess dispersion conditional on the fitted mean rather than comparing only raw overall counts. Extra variation may indicate that the model assumptions are inadequate.

lessons.title: Consider overdispersion
lessons.body: Negative-binomial models can allow conditional variance greater than the mean. They are one possible response to overdispersion, not an automatic fix for omitted variables, dependence, or other data issues.

lessons.title: Evaluate the model
lessons.body: Use held-out data and diagnostics suited to the count task. Inspect residual patterns, exposure, and uncertainty, and compare a suitable baseline. Check whether sampling, dependence, or excess zeros require a different model.

topics.title: Quantile regression
topics.description: Quantile regression estimates conditional quantiles, supporting asymmetric risk and service-level planning.

lessons.title: Predict a conditional quantile
lessons.body: A conditional quantile describes a point in the distribution of an outcome for inputs like the current case. For example, a 0.9 quantile of delivery time is a value at or below which approximately 90% of comparable delivery times fall. Unlike a mean, it is useful for questions about the upper tail. This interpretation depends on the model and the data; an individual prediction is not a guaranteed deadline.

lessons.title: Train with asymmetric loss
lessons.body: For a target quantile q, define the residual as actual minus prediction. Pinball loss is q times the residual when the residual is nonnegative, and (q - 1) times the residual otherwise. At q = 0.9, underpredicting by one unit costs 0.9 while overpredicting by one unit costs 0.1. Minimizing this loss targets the conditional q quantile rather than the conditional mean.

lessons.title: Match the quantile to the decision
lessons.body: An upper quantile can inform a delivery buffer when an underestimate is more costly than an overestimate. A lower quantile can be useful when the cost trade-off is reversed. The right level depends on the decision and the relative costs; choosing 0.9 does not automatically give an optimal policy. Confirm that the training targets and available features match how predictions will be used.

lessons.title: Evaluate on held-out outcomes
lessons.body: On held-out examples, report pinball loss at the chosen quantile and the fraction of outcomes at or below the prediction. For a well-calibrated continuous conditional distribution, that fraction should be near the chosen quantile; ties and discrete outcomes complicate this comparison. Check important groups and time periods separately, and account for sampling uncertainty rather than relying on one aggregate rate.

lessons.title: Check intervals and changing data
lessons.body: Predictions at a lower and an upper quantile can form an estimated interval, but independently fitted quantiles can cross and their nominal levels do not by themselves guarantee future coverage. Measure both observed coverage and interval width on held-out data, including relevant groups. Monitor those measures after deployment because changes in the population or measurement process can make earlier results unreliable.

topics.title: Monotonic constraints
topics.description: Monotonic constraints encode trusted directional relationships and can improve plausibility without proving causality.

lessons.title: Core idea and practice
lessons.body: Monotonic constraints encode trusted directional relationships and can improve plausibility without proving causality. Constrain risk score to not decrease as a known risk factor increases. This distinction should be checked against the data, users, and constraints of the actual task rather than treated as a guarantee.

lessons.title: State the direction precisely
lessons.body: A monotonic constraint requires predictions to move only in a specified direction as one feature changes, holding the model's other inputs fixed. It does not require a constant rate of change.

lessons.title: Validate the domain assumption
lessons.body: Confirm the direction with domain evidence across the intended population and inspect whether interactions make it inappropriate. A constraint can improve plausibility, but it does not establish a causal relationship.

topics.title: Model explainability limits
topics.description: Feature importance and local explanations describe model behavior under chosen definitions; they are not causal explanations.

lessons.title: Core idea and practice
lessons.body: Feature importance and local explanations describe model behavior under chosen definitions; they are not causal explanations. Use explanations to generate audit questions, then verify with independent analysis. This distinction should be checked against the data, users, and constraints of the actual task rather than treated as a guarantee.

lessons.title: Know what an explanation describes
lessons.body: Feature importance depends on the chosen importance definition and can be distorted by correlated inputs. A local attribution describes how a particular model output was decomposed, not what would happen under an intervention.

lessons.title: Use explanations as audit leads
lessons.body: Check explanations against data provenance, counterexamples, and domain knowledge, and test stability under reasonable perturbations. Do not treat a plausible attribution as proof that the model is fair or causally correct.

topics.title: Out-of-time validation
topics.description: Temporal validation estimates future-facing performance when data and relationships evolve over time.

lessons.title: Core idea and practice
lessons.body: Temporal validation estimates future-facing performance when data and relationships evolve over time. Train on earlier periods and test on a later period with a gap for delayed labels. This distinction should be checked against the data, users, and constraints of the actual task rather than treated as a guarantee.

lessons.title: Design a forward-looking split
lessons.body: Train on earlier periods and test on a later period that represents the deployment horizon. Add a gap or purge overlapping records when labels or features span time across the boundary.

lessons.title: Measure temporal degradation
lessons.body: Report performance across multiple historical cutoffs and compare cohorts, seasonality, and data availability. A single future holdout estimates one period and cannot guarantee performance in every later regime.

topics.title: Online experimentation
topics.description: Randomized experiments estimate intervention effects when assignment and exposure are controlled.

lessons.title: Core idea and practice
lessons.body: Randomized experiments estimate intervention effects when assignment and exposure are controlled. Pre-register a primary outcome and guardrail before an A/B test. This distinction should be checked against the data, users, and constraints of the actual task rather than treated as a guarantee.

lessons.title: Define the experiment before exposure
lessons.body: Specify the target population, randomization unit, primary outcome, duration, and guardrails before examining treatment results. The unit should prevent interference when one participant's assignment affects another's outcome.

lessons.title: Interpret the effect and safety checks
lessons.body: Analyze participants by assigned group and account for the experiment's design. Check exposure, missing outcomes, and guardrails before deciding whether an observed average effect supports deployment.

topics.title: Selective prediction
topics.description: A model can abstain on uncertain cases, trading coverage for improved accuracy on accepted predictions.

lessons.title: Core idea and practice
lessons.body: A model can abstain on uncertain cases, trading coverage for improved accuracy on accepted predictions. Route low-confidence medical coding cases to a human reviewer. This distinction should be checked against the data, users, and constraints of the actual task rather than treated as a guarantee.

lessons.title: Define coverage and risk
lessons.body: Coverage is the fraction of cases on which the model makes an accepted prediction; selective risk is error among those accepted cases. An abstention rule trades lower coverage for potentially lower accepted-case error.

lessons.title: Design a safe fallback
lessons.body: Set an abstention policy using validation data and route rejected cases to a qualified fallback, such as human review. Monitor both accepted-case errors and the volume and composition of abstentions.

topics.title: Privacy-aware learning
topics.description: Privacy mechanisms limit information disclosed about training examples, with a measurable utility and privacy trade-off.

lessons.title: Core idea and practice
lessons.body: Privacy mechanisms limit information disclosed about training examples, with a measurable utility and privacy trade-off. Track a differential-privacy budget across repeated training releases. This distinction should be checked against the data, users, and constraints of the actual task rather than treated as a guarantee.

lessons.title: Track the privacy guarantee
lessons.body: Differential privacy bounds how much a released result can change when one person's data is added or removed, under a stated neighboring-dataset definition. The privacy budget composes across repeated releases and training runs.

lessons.title: Balance privacy and utility
lessons.body: Document the threat model, privacy parameters, and utility costs, and limit access to sensitive raw data. A privacy guarantee does not by itself eliminate all security, fairness, or governance risks.

topics.title: Fairness constraints
topics.description: Fairness criteria can conflict and may be mathematically incompatible under unequal base rates.

lessons.title: Core idea and practice
lessons.body: Fairness criteria can conflict and may be mathematically incompatible under unequal base rates. Choose a criterion based on the harms and document the trade-off. This distinction should be checked against the data, users, and constraints of the actual task rather than treated as a guarantee.

lessons.title: Specify the criterion and population
lessons.body: A parity constraint is meaningful only after defining the outcome, groups, and population to which it applies. Different criteria such as equalized error rates and predictive parity encode different priorities.

lessons.title: Expose incompatible demands
lessons.body: With unequal base rates and imperfect prediction, some group fairness criteria cannot generally all hold at once. Quantify the conflict, discuss harms with affected stakeholders, and document the chosen trade-off.

topics.title: Model cards and datasheets
topics.description: Structured documentation records intended use, evaluation scope, data provenance, and known limitations.

lessons.title: Core idea and practice
lessons.body: Structured documentation records intended use, evaluation scope, data provenance, and known limitations. Publish subgroup results and deployment exclusions with the model artifact. This distinction should be checked against the data, users, and constraints of the actual task rather than treated as a guarantee.

lessons.title: Record evidence and boundaries
lessons.body: A model card should state intended use, evaluation design, subgroup performance, limitations, and prohibited uses. A dataset datasheet should document provenance, collection, labeling, and known gaps.

lessons.title: Keep documentation connected to release
lessons.body: Version documentation with the model and update it when data, thresholds, or deployment context changes. Clear exclusions help downstream users avoid assuming the model is validated for every population.

topics.title: Decommissioning models
topics.description: Retirement requires replacing downstream dependencies, preserving audit records, and stopping stale predictions.

lessons.title: Core idea and practice
lessons.body: Retirement requires replacing downstream dependencies, preserving audit records, and stopping stale predictions. Define a rollback and consumer-notification plan before removing a model. This distinction should be checked against the data, users, and constraints of the actual task rather than treated as a guarantee.

lessons.title: Map dependencies before shutdown
lessons.body: Identify applications, scheduled jobs, cached outputs, and human workflows that depend on the model. Plan a supported replacement or fallback so that removing the service does not silently disrupt decisions.

lessons.title: Retire with traceability
lessons.body: Stop new predictions, notify consumers, preserve records needed for audits under appropriate retention rules, and verify that stale outputs are no longer used. Monitor the transition and document the final shutdown date.
